Results

General Summary

Across the entire study, squirrels experienced an average local density of `r round(mean(dat$density), 1)` ± `r round(sd(dat$density), 1)` squirrels/ha. Food supplementation increased the local density around mothers on food add grids at a rate of `r round((dat[food == 1 & year == 2017, mean(density)] - dat[food == 1 & year == 2005, mean(density)])/12, 2)` squirrel per hectare per year over the 12 years of its food experiment. Over the entire study, mothers on food supplemented grids experienced higher local densities, with an average of `r dat[food == 1, round(mean(density), 2)]` squirrels/ha, compared to those on control grids, that had on average `r dat[food == 0, round(mean(density), 2)]` squirrels/ha. Mothers on rattle treatment grids had the lowest densities at `r dat[food == 19, round(mean(density), 2)]` squirrels/ha (Figure 1A). However, there was substantial natural variation in local densities over time (Figure 2B). Pups grew at a rate of `r round(mean(dat$growthrate), 1)` ± `r round(sd(dat$growthrate), 1)` g/day, with litters from bucket middens have slightly higher average growth rates at `r dat[treatment_ind == "Bucket", round(mean(growthrate), 1)]` ± `r dat[treatment_ind == "Bucket", round(sd(growthrate), 1)]` g/day (Figure 1C). Litters had `r round(mean(dat$littersize))` pups on average, but could range anywhere from `r min(dat$littersize)` to `r max(dat$littersize)` pups (Figure 1D). Based on data from control grids, with every pup increase in litter size, litter growth rate decreased `r abs(gr_ls_slope)` g/day (Figure 2). The most common age for mothers was `r getmode(dat$mother_age)` years, and litters were born on average at `r round(mean(dat$bjulian))` ± `r round(sd(dat$bjulian))` Julian days into the year.
